# Introduction to German: Three Genders, Articles, and Greetings

## The German Language

German (Deutsch) is spoken by approximately 130 million people as a native or second language. It is the official language of Germany, Austria, Switzerland (alongside French, Italian, and Romansh), Liechtenstein, and Luxembourg. German is the most widely spoken native language in the European Union.

## Three Grammatical Genders

Unlike Spanish or French with two genders, German has THREE: masculine (der), feminine (die), and neuter (das). The gender of a noun must be memorized with each word, as there are many exceptions to any "rules."

**General tendencies (not absolute rules):**

| Gender | Typical Endings | Examples |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| Masculine (der) | -er, -ling, -ismus, -or | der Lehrer (teacher), der Frühling (spring), der Tourismus, der Motor |
| Feminine (die) | -ung, -heit, -keit, -tion, -ie, -schaft, -tät | die Zeitung (newspaper), die Freiheit (freedom), die Möglichkeit (possibility), die Nation, die Energie, die Freundschaft (friendship), die Universität |
| Neuter (das) | -chen, -lein, -ment, -um, Ge- | das Mädchen (girl — neuter!), das Büchlein (little book), das Dokument, das Datum, das Gebäude (building) |

**Important exceptions:** das Mädchen (the girl) is NEUTER because the diminutive suffix -chen always makes a word neuter, regardless of natural gender.

## Articles

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter | Plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Definite (the) | der | die | das | die |
| Indefinite (a) | ein | eine | ein | — (no plural) |

The plural definite article is always **die** regardless of the singular gender.

## Plural Formation

German plurals are more complex than in most languages. There are several patterns:

| Pattern | Example |
|---------|---------|
| Add -e | der Tisch → die Tische (tables) |
| Add -er (often with umlaut) | das Kind → die Kinder (children) |
| Add -en/-n | die Lampe → die Lampen (lamps) |
| Add -s (foreign words) | das Auto → die Autos (cars) |
| No change (often with umlaut) | der Vater → die Väter (fathers) |
| Add umlaut + -e | der Stuhl → die Stühle (chairs) |

**Tip:** Always learn the plural form when you learn a new noun: der Tisch, -e.

## Basic Sentence Structure

German main clauses follow a strict rule: **the conjugated verb always occupies the second position** (V2 rule).

- Ich lerne Deutsch. (I learn German.)
- Heute lerne ich Deutsch. (Today I learn German. — "heute" is first, so the verb stays second and the subject moves after it)
- Der Mann liest ein Buch. (The man reads a book.)

## All Nouns Are Capitalized

Unlike other European languages, German capitalizes ALL nouns, not just proper nouns:
- Ich lese ein **B**uch in der **S**chule. (I read a book in school.)
- Der **H**und spielt im **G**arten. (The dog plays in the garden.)

## Common Greetings

| German | English | When/Where |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| Hallo | Hello | Universal, informal |
| Guten Morgen | Good morning | Until ~10 AM |
| Guten Tag | Good day | Standard, anytime |
| Guten Abend | Good evening | Evening |
| Gute Nacht | Good night | Bedtime only |
| Auf Wiedersehen | Goodbye | Formal |
| Tschüss | Bye | Informal |
| Bis bald | See you soon | Universal |
| Bis morgen | See you tomorrow | Universal |
| Grüß Gott | Hello (greeting God) | Southern Germany, Austria |
| Servus | Hello/Bye | Bavaria, Austria |
| Moin | Hello | Northern Germany |

## Pronunciation Basics

| Letter/Combo | Pronunciation | Example |
|-------------|--------------|---------|
| ä | like "eh" in "bet" | Mädchen |
| ö | like French "eu" — round lips and say "eh" | schön (beautiful) |
| ü | like French "u" — round lips and say "ee" | über (over) |
| ß (Eszett) | like "ss" | Straße (street) |
| ch (after a,o,u) | guttural, like Scottish "loch" | Buch (book) |
| ch (after e,i) | soft, like "sh" without the "s" | ich (I) |
| w | like English "v" | Wasser (water) |
| v | like English "f" | Vater (father) |
| z | like "ts" | Zeit (time) |
| ei | like English "eye" | mein (my) |
| ie | like English "ee" | die (the) |
| eu/äu | like "oy" | deutsch, Häuser |

## Practice

Write five sentences introducing yourself: Ich heiße... Ich bin... Jahre alt. Ich komme aus... Ich wohne in... Ich lerne Deutsch.

**Practice and Application**

Mastering German requires consistent engagement with the language across all four skills: reading, writing, listening, and speaking. German has a reputation among English speakers as being difficult, but this reputation is somewhat misleading. While German grammar is more complex than English in certain respects (three genders, four cases, complex word order rules, and extensive verb conjugation), the two languages share Germanic roots that provide a substantial foundation of cognate vocabulary and structural similarities. English speakers who approach German systematically can leverage these similarities while focusing their efforts on the areas of genuine difference.

Vocabulary acquisition is supported by the systematic nature of German word formation. German is famous for its compound nouns (Zusammensetzungen), which combine two or more words into a single, often lengthy word whose meaning can usually be deduced from its components. For example, Handschuh (glove) literally means hand-shoe, Staubsauger (vacuum cleaner) means dust-sucker, and Krankenversicherung (health insurance) means sick-insurance. Understanding the component-building principle allows learners to decode unfamiliar compound words and to recognize the semantic relationships between related words. German also uses a highly productive system of prefixes and suffixes to create new words from existing roots, further expanding the learner's ability to deduce meaning from word structure.

Pronunciation in German is generally more regular and predictable than in English. Once the sound values of individual letters and letter combinations are learned, most words can be pronounced correctly on sight, unlike English where spelling-to-pronunciation correspondence is notoriously inconsistent. Key pronunciation features that require specific attention from English speakers include the umlauted vowels (ae, oe, ue), the ch sound (which has two variants: the palatal ich-Laut after front vowels and consonants, and the velar ach-Laut after back vowels), the r sound (typically a uvular fricative or trill, quite different from the English r), and the distinction between long and short vowels (which is phonemic in German, meaning it changes word meaning: Staat/state versus Stadt/city).

The case system (Nominativ, Akkusativ, Dativ, Genitiv) is often cited as the most challenging aspect of German grammar for English speakers. Cases indicate the grammatical function of nouns and pronouns in a sentence (subject, direct object, indirect object, possession), and they affect the forms of articles, adjectives, and pronouns. English retains vestiges of a case system in pronouns (I/me/my, he/him/his, who/whom/whose), but German applies case distinctions systematically across all nouns and their modifiers. The key to mastering cases is understanding their functional logic rather than simply memorizing tables: the nominative identifies the subject (who or what does the action), the accusative identifies the direct object (who or what receives the action), the dative identifies the indirect object (to or for whom), and the genitive indicates possession (whose). Many prepositions require specific cases, and the two-way prepositions (Wechselpraepositionen: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, ueber, unter, vor, zwischen) take either accusative (indicating motion toward) or dative (indicating location at), depending on the meaning intended.

**Cultural Connections**

German language learning is enriched by engagement with the diverse cultures of the German-speaking world (DACH countries: Deutschland/Germany, Oesterreich/Austria, and die Schweiz/Switzerland, plus Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, parts of Belgium, and South Tyrol in Italy). These regions share a common language but have distinct cultural identities, customs, dialects, and culinary traditions. Understanding these cultural dimensions enhances language learning by providing authentic contexts for vocabulary and grammar, motivating continued study through cultural interest, and developing intercultural competence that is valuable in personal and professional contexts.

German-speaking countries have made enormous contributions to world culture in philosophy (Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Wittgenstein, Heidegger), music (Bach, Beethoven, Mozart, Wagner, Strauss, Schoenberg), literature (Goethe, Schiller, Kafka, Mann, Hesse, Rilke), science (Einstein, Heisenberg, Planck, Koch, Roentgen), and psychology (Freud, Jung). Engaging with these cultural contributions in their original language provides deeper understanding and appreciation than translation alone can offer.

# Numbers, Days, Months, and Colors

## Numbers 1-100

**1-12 (memorize individually):**
1 = eins, 2 = zwei, 3 = drei, 4 = vier, 5 = fünf, 6 = sechs, 7 = sieben, 8 = acht, 9 = neun, 10 = zehn, 11 = elf, 12 = zwölf

**13-19 (ones + zehn):**
13 = dreizehn, 14 = vierzehn, 15 = fünfzehn, 16 = sechzehn (note: "sechs" loses the "s"), 17 = siebzehn (note: "sieben" loses "en"), 18 = achtzehn, 19 = neunzehn

**20-99 (ONES first, then "und" + tens — reverse of English!):**
20 = zwanzig, 21 = ein**und**zwanzig (literally "one-and-twenty"), 22 = zweiundzwanzig, 30 = dreißig, 40 = vierzig, 50 = fünfzig, 60 = sechzig, 70 = siebzig, 80 = achtzig, 90 = neunzig, 100 = (ein)hundert

**Key pattern:** German says the ones digit BEFORE the tens: 54 = vierundfünfzig (four-and-fifty), 87 = siebenundachtzig (seven-and-eighty). This takes practice!

**Larger numbers:** 200 = zweihundert, 1.000 = (ein)tausend, 1.000.000 = eine Million. Note: German uses periods for thousands and commas for decimals (opposite of English): 1.500,50 = one thousand five hundred point fifty.

## Days of the Week

All days are masculine (der) and capitalized:

| German | English | Etymology |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| (der) Montag | Monday | Mond (moon) |
| (der) Dienstag | Tuesday | Service/duty day |
| (der) Mittwoch | Wednesday | Mid-week |
| (der) Donnerstag | Thursday | Donner (thunder — Thor) |
| (der) Freitag | Friday | Freya (Norse goddess) |
| (der) Samstag / Sonnabend | Saturday | Sabbath / Sun-evening |
| (der) Sonntag | Sunday | Sonne (sun) |

"On Monday" = am Montag. "On Mondays" (habitual) = montags (lowercase, no article).

## Months

All months are masculine (der) and capitalized:
(der) Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni, Juli, August, September, Oktober, November, Dezember

"In January" = im Januar (im = in dem).

## Dates

- Der wievielte ist heute? / Welches Datum haben wir? (What is today's date?)
- Heute ist der dritte März. (Today is March 3rd.) — ordinal numbers are used
- Ordinal numbers: 1.-19. add -te: der erste (1st), der zweite (2nd), der dritte (3rd), der vierte (4th)... 20+ add -ste: der zwanzigste, der einunddreißigste
- Written format: 3.3.2025 or 03.03.2025 (day.month.year)

## Colors (Die Farben)

Colors are adjectives. When used after sein (to be), they do not decline. Before a noun, they take adjective endings (covered later).

| German | English |
|--------|---------|
| rot | red |
| blau | blue |
| grün | green |
| gelb | yellow |
| schwarz | black |
| weiß | white |
| braun | brown |
| grau | gray |
| rosa | pink |
| orange | orange |
| lila / violett | purple |
| dunkelblau | dark blue |
| hellgrün | light green |

**After sein:** Das Auto ist rot. (The car is red.) Die Blume ist gelb. (The flower is yellow.)

**Before a noun (with adjective endings):** ein rotes Auto (a red car), eine gelbe Blume (a yellow flower) — adjective endings will be covered in the grammar section.

## Practice

Practice saying: Heute ist der... (today's date). Count from 1 to 100. Say your birthday: Mein Geburtstag ist am... (My birthday is on the...). Describe five objects by color: Das Buch ist blau. Die Tasche ist schwarz.

# Introductions, Personal Information, and Polite Phrases

## Introducing Yourself

**Name:**
- Ich heiße Anna. (My name is Anna. — literally "I am called Anna")
- Mein Name ist Anna. (My name is Anna. — more formal)
- Ich bin Anna. (I am Anna. — casual)

**Age:**
- Ich bin fünfzehn Jahre alt. (I am fifteen years old.)
- German uses "sein" (to be) for age, unlike Spanish/French which use "to have."

**Origin:**
- Ich komme aus Deutschland. (I come from Germany.)
- Ich bin Deutsche / Deutscher. (I am German. — feminine / masculine)
- Ich bin Amerikaner / Amerikanerin. (I am American.)

**Residence:**
- Ich wohne in Berlin. (I live in Berlin.)
- Ich lebe in den USA. (I live in the USA.)

**Occupation/School:**
- Ich bin Schüler / Schülerin. (I am a student — school level.)
- Ich bin Student / Studentin. (I am a student — university level.)
- Ich gehe in die zehnte Klasse. (I am in tenth grade.)
- Ich arbeite als Ingenieur. (I work as an engineer.)

**Hobbies:**
- Meine Hobbys sind Lesen und Sport. (My hobbies are reading and sports.)
- In meiner Freizeit spiele ich Fußball. (In my free time I play soccer.)
- Ich lerne gern Deutsch. (I like learning German.)

## Sample Introduction

"Hallo! Ich heiße Thomas und bin sechzehn Jahre alt. Ich komme aus München in Deutschland, aber jetzt wohne ich in Hamburg. Ich bin Schüler am Gymnasium Friedrich Schiller. Meine Lieblingsfächer sind Mathematik und Physik. In meiner Freizeit spiele ich Gitarre und lese gern Bücher. Freut mich!"

(Hello! My name is Thomas and I am sixteen years old. I come from Munich in Germany, but now I live in Hamburg. I am a student at Friedrich Schiller Gymnasium. My favorite subjects are math and physics. In my free time I play guitar and like to read books. Nice to meet you!)

## Common Questions

| German | English | Register |
|--------|---------|----------|
| Wie heißen Sie? / Wie heißt du? | What is your name? | Formal / Informal |
| Woher kommen Sie? / Woher kommst du? | Where do you come from? | Formal / Informal |
| Wo wohnen Sie? / Wo wohnst du? | Where do you live? | Formal / Informal |
| Wie alt sind Sie? / Wie alt bist du? | How old are you? | Formal / Informal |
| Was machen Sie beruflich? / Was machst du? | What do you do (for work)? | Formal / Informal |
| Was sind Ihre Hobbys? / Was sind deine Hobbys? | What are your hobbies? | Formal / Informal |
| Sprechen Sie Deutsch? / Sprichst du Deutsch? | Do you speak German? | Formal / Informal |

## Polite Expressions

| German | English |
|--------|---------|
| Bitte | Please / You're welcome |
| Danke / Danke schön / Vielen Dank | Thanks / Thank you / Many thanks |
| Bitte schön / Gern geschehen | You're welcome |
| Entschuldigung / Entschuldigen Sie | Excuse me |
| Es tut mir leid | I'm sorry |
| Kein Problem | No problem |
| Freut mich | Nice to meet you |
| Sehr erfreut | Very pleased (formal) |
| Gleichfalls | Likewise |
| Prost! / Zum Wohl! | Cheers! |
| Guten Appetit! | Enjoy your meal! |
| Gesundheit! | Bless you! (after sneezing) |

## Du vs. Sie

This distinction is extremely important in German culture:
- **Sie** (formal you — always capitalized): Use with strangers, elders, authority figures, in professional settings, in shops and restaurants. Conjugates like third-person plural.
- **du** (informal you — lowercase): Use with friends, family, children, animals, and people who offer it. Uses second-person singular conjugation.

**Offering the du:** An older or higher-status person may say "Wir können uns duzen" (We can use du with each other) or "Sag ruhig du zu mir" (Feel free to say du to me). It is NEVER appropriate to initiate this switch yourself with someone of higher status.

In modern German workplaces, especially in tech and startups, du is increasingly common. Traditional industries (law, banking, government) still use Sie extensively.

## Practice

Write your own introduction paragraph following the model. Include: name, age, origin, residence, school/work, favorite subjects or activities, and one hobby. Practice both the du and Sie forms of common questions.

# Family Vocabulary and Possessive Articles

## Family Members (Die Familie)

| German | English | Gender |
|--------|---------|--------|
| die Mutter / die Mama | mother / mom | F |
| der Vater / der Papa | father / dad | M |
| die Eltern (pl.) | parents | — |
| der Bruder | brother | M |
| die Schwester | sister | F |
| die Geschwister (pl.) | siblings | — |
| der Sohn | son | M |
| die Tochter | daughter | F |
| die Kinder (pl.) | children | — |
| der Großvater / der Opa | grandfather / grandpa | M |
| die Großmutter / die Oma | grandmother / grandma | F |
| die Großeltern (pl.) | grandparents | — |
| der Onkel | uncle | M |
| die Tante | aunt | F |
| der Cousin / die Cousine | cousin (m./f.) | M/F |
| der Neffe | nephew | M |
| die Nichte | niece | F |
| der Enkel / die Enkelin | grandson / granddaughter | M/F |
| der Schwiegervater / die Schwiegermutter | father-in-law / mother-in-law | M/F |
| der Schwager / die Schwägerin | brother-in-law / sister-in-law | M/F |
| der Ehemann / der Mann | husband | M |
| die Ehefrau / die Frau | wife | F |
| der Freund / die Freundin | boyfriend / girlfriend (or friend) | M/F |
| das Einzelkind | only child | N |
| die Zwillinge (pl.) | twins | — |

## Possessive Articles (Possessivartikel)

German possessive articles function like the indefinite article "ein" — they take the same endings based on the gender, number, and case of the noun they precede.

**Base forms (Nominative case):**

| Person | Base | Before Masc. (der) | Before Fem. (die) | Before Neut. (das) | Before Plural |
|--------|------|-------|------|------|--------|
| ich (my) | mein | mein Vater | meine Mutter | mein Kind | meine Kinder |
| du (your) | dein | dein Vater | deine Mutter | dein Kind | deine Kinder |
| er (his) | sein | sein Vater | seine Mutter | sein Kind | seine Kinder |
| sie (her) | ihr | ihr Vater | ihre Mutter | ihr Kind | ihre Kinder |
| es (its) | sein | sein Vater | seine Mutter | sein Kind | seine Kinder |
| wir (our) | unser | unser Vater | unsere Mutter | unser Kind | unsere Kinder |
| ihr (your pl.) | euer | euer Vater | eure Mutter | euer Kind | eure Kinder |
| sie/Sie (their/Your) | ihr/Ihr | ihr Vater | ihre Mutter | ihr Kind | ihre Kinder |

**Key points:**
- Masculine and neuter singular: no ending (mein Vater, mein Kind)
- Feminine singular and all plurals: add -e (meine Mutter, meine Kinder)
- "euer" drops the middle -e when an ending is added: eure (not "euere")
- Possessive articles agree with the THING POSSESSED, not the possessor

**Examples:**
- Mein Bruder heißt Max. (My brother is called Max.)
- Meine Schwester ist zwölf Jahre alt. (My sister is twelve years old.)
- Unsere Großeltern wohnen in München. (Our grandparents live in Munich.)
- Ihre Kinder gehen in die Schule. (Her/Their children go to school.)

## Talking About Family

- Ich habe eine große Familie mit drei Geschwistern. (I have a big family with three siblings.)
- Mein älterer Bruder studiert an der Universität. (My older brother studies at university.)
- Meine jüngere Schwester ist noch in der Grundschule. (My younger sister is still in elementary school.)
- Wir sind fünf Personen in meiner Familie. (There are five people in my family.)
- Meine Eltern arbeiten beide. (My parents both work.)

## Cultural Note

German family structures have evolved significantly. While traditional families remain common, there is strong legal protection for diverse family forms. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2017. The concept of "Elternzeit" (parental leave) allows either parent to take extended leave, and fathers increasingly take advantage of this.

## Practice

Describe your family in German using possessive articles. Write at least six sentences: Meine Mutter heißt... Mein Vater arbeitet als... Meine Geschwister sind... Unsere Familie wohnt in...

# Food, Meals, and Restaurant Vocabulary

## German Meals (Die Mahlzeiten)

| German | English | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| das Frühstück | breakfast | Typically 6-9 AM. Bread, rolls, cheese, cold cuts, jam, eggs, coffee. Germany is famous for its breakfast culture. |
| das Mittagessen | lunch | 12-1 PM. Traditionally the main hot meal. |
| die Kaffeepause / Kaffee und Kuchen | coffee break | 3-4 PM. Coffee and cake — a beloved German tradition. |
| das Abendessen / das Abendbrot | dinner / evening bread | 6-8 PM. Often cold: bread, cheese, cold cuts (Aufschnitt). |

## Food Vocabulary

**Bread and Baked Goods (das Brot und Gebäck):**
Germany has over 3,200 registered bread varieties — more than any country!
das Brot (bread), das Brötchen / die Semmel (roll), das Vollkornbrot (whole grain bread), das Roggenbrot (rye bread), die Brezel / die Bretzel (pretzel), der Kuchen (cake), die Torte (layer cake/tart)

**Proteins:** das Fleisch (meat), das Schweinefleisch (pork — most popular), das Rindfleisch (beef), das Hühnchen / das Hähnchen (chicken), der Fisch (fish), die Wurst (sausage), der Schinken (ham), das Ei / die Eier (egg/eggs)

**Dairy:** die Milch (milk), der Käse (cheese), die Butter (butter), der Joghurt (yogurt), die Sahne (cream), der Quark (a fresh dairy product unique to German cuisine)

**Vegetables:** das Gemüse (vegetables), die Kartoffel (potato), die Tomate (tomato), die Zwiebel (onion), der Kohl (cabbage), die Gurke (cucumber), die Karotte / die Möhre (carrot), die Erbse (pea), der Pilz (mushroom), der Spargel (asparagus — Germans are obsessed with asparagus season!)

**Fruits:** das Obst (fruit), der Apfel (apple), die Birne (pear), die Erdbeere (strawberry), die Kirsche (cherry), die Traube (grape), die Banane (banana), die Orange / die Apfelsine (orange)

**Drinks:** das Wasser (water), der Kaffee (coffee), der Tee (tea), der Saft (juice), das Bier (beer), der Wein (wine), die Limonade (lemon soda), der Apfelsaft (apple juice), die Milch (milk)

## At a Restaurant (Im Restaurant)

| German | English |
|--------|---------|
| Einen Tisch für zwei, bitte. | A table for two, please. |
| Die Speisekarte, bitte. / Die Karte, bitte. | The menu, please. |
| Was empfehlen Sie? | What do you recommend? |
| Ich möchte bitte... / Ich hätte gern... | I would like... |
| Für mich das Schnitzel, bitte. | The schnitzel for me, please. |
| Haben Sie etwas Vegetarisches? | Do you have something vegetarian? |
| Die Rechnung, bitte. | The check, please. |
| Zusammen oder getrennt? | Together or separate? |
| Getrennt, bitte. | Separate, please. |
| Stimmt so. | Keep the change. |
| Guten Appetit! | Enjoy your meal! |
| Prost! / Zum Wohl! | Cheers! |
| Es schmeckt sehr gut! | It tastes very good! |

**Taste descriptions:** lecker (delicious), scharf (spicy), süß (sweet), salzig (salty), bitter (bitter), sauer (sour), würzig (savory/spiced), mild (mild), frisch (fresh)

## Iconic German Foods

- **Bratwurst:** Grilled sausage, countless regional varieties
- **Schnitzel:** Breaded and fried cutlet (Wiener Schnitzel = veal)
- **Sauerkraut:** Fermented cabbage
- **Kartoffelsalat:** Potato salad (varies by region)
- **Spätzle:** Egg noodles (Swabian specialty)
- **Döner Kebab:** Turkish-German fast food, a Berlin institution
- **Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte:** Black Forest cherry cake
- **Stollen:** Christmas fruit bread

## Cultural Note on Dining

Tipping in Germany: Round up the bill or add 5-10%. Tell the server the total you want to pay: if the bill is €17.50, say "Neunzehn, bitte" (Nineteen, please) when paying. Do NOT leave money on the table — hand it directly to the server.

Water is not automatically free. You will be asked "Mit Gas oder ohne Gas?" (with or without carbonation). Tap water (Leitungswasser) can be requested but is uncommon.

## Practice

Write a restaurant dialogue: greeting, ordering a drink, asking for a recommendation, ordering food, commenting on the taste, and paying.

# Telling Time and Weather

## Telling Time (Die Uhrzeit)

**Asking:** Wie spät ist es? / Wie viel Uhr ist es? (What time is it?)

**Stating the time:**
- Es ist ein Uhr. (It's one o'clock.)
- Es ist drei Uhr. (It's three o'clock.)

**The tricky part — half hours:**
In German, "halb" refers to half TO the NEXT hour, not half past:
- **halb vier** = 3:30 (half to four, NOT half four/4:30!)
- **halb zwölf** = 11:30

This is the single most confusing aspect of German time for English speakers. Always remember: halb + next hour.

**Quarter hours:**
- Viertel nach drei = 3:15 (quarter past three)
- Viertel vor vier = 3:45 (quarter to four)

**Minutes:**
- fünf nach drei = 3:05
- zehn nach drei = 3:10
- zwanzig nach drei = 3:20
- fünf vor halb vier = 3:25 (five before half-to-four)
- fünf nach halb vier = 3:35 (five after half-to-four)
- zehn vor vier = 3:50
- fünf vor vier = 3:55

**Time of day:**
morgens (in the morning), vormittags (mid-morning), mittags (at noon), nachmittags (in the afternoon), abends (in the evening), nachts (at night)

**24-hour clock:** Used in formal contexts, schedules, and transportation:
- Der Zug fährt um fünfzehn Uhr dreißig. (The train departs at 15:30.)

**Useful expressions:**
- Um wie viel Uhr? (At what time?)
- Um acht Uhr. (At eight o'clock.)
- Punkt acht (at eight sharp)
- gegen acht (around eight)
- früh (early), spät (late), pünktlich (on time)

## Weather (Das Wetter)

**Asking:** Wie ist das Wetter? / Wie ist das Wetter heute? (How is the weather? / How is the weather today?)

**Weather with "es ist":**
| German | English |
|--------|---------|
| Es ist heiß. | It's hot. |
| Es ist warm. | It's warm. |
| Es ist kühl. | It's cool. |
| Es ist kalt. | It's cold. |
| Es ist sonnig. | It's sunny. |
| Es ist bewölkt. | It's cloudy. |
| Es ist windig. | It's windy. |
| Es ist neblig. | It's foggy. |
| Es ist schwül. | It's humid/muggy. |

**Weather with verbs:**
| German | English |
|--------|---------|
| Es regnet. | It's raining. |
| Es schneit. | It's snowing. |
| Es hagelt. | It's hailing. |
| Es donnert und blitzt. | It's thundering and lightning. |
| Die Sonne scheint. | The sun is shining. |

**Temperature:**
- Wie viel Grad sind es? / Wie viel Grad hat es? (How many degrees is it?)
- Es sind zwanzig Grad. (It's 20 degrees.)
- Es sind minus fünf Grad. (It's -5 degrees.)
- Germany uses Celsius.

**Seasons (Die Jahreszeiten):**
der Frühling (spring), der Sommer (summer), der Herbst (fall/autumn), der Winter (winter)
- im Frühling (in spring), im Sommer (in summer)
- Im Winter ist es kalt und es schneit oft. (In winter it's cold and it often snows.)
- Im Sommer ist es warm und die Sonne scheint. (In summer it's warm and the sun shines.)

## Practice

Write dialogues asking and answering about time and weather. Practice the "halb" construction especially:
- Wie spät ist es? — Es ist halb sieben. (6:30)
- Wie ist das Wetter? — Es regnet, aber es ist nicht kalt.

# Present Tense: Regular Verbs

## Verb Conjugation Basics

German verbs in the infinitive end in -en (or sometimes -n): spielen (to play), machen (to do/make), arbeiten (to work). To conjugate, remove -en to find the stem, then add personal endings.

**Model: SPIELEN (to play)**

| Person | Pronoun | Stem + Ending | Form |
|--------|---------|--------------|------|
| 1st sing. | ich | spiel + e | spiele |
| 2nd sing. informal | du | spiel + st | spielst |
| 3rd sing. | er/sie/es | spiel + t | spielt |
| 1st plural | wir | spiel + en | spielen |
| 2nd pl. informal | ihr | spiel + t | spielt |
| 3rd plural / formal | sie/Sie | spiel + en | spielen |

**Endings: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en**

Note: wir, sie (they), and Sie (formal you) forms are always identical to the infinitive.

## Common Regular Verbs

| Infinitive | English | Example |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| lernen | to learn | Ich lerne Deutsch. |
| machen | to do/make | Was machst du? (What are you doing?) |
| wohnen | to live | Wir wohnen in Berlin. |
| kaufen | to buy | Sie kauft ein neues Buch. |
| hören | to hear/listen | Er hört Musik. |
| sagen | to say | Was sagt er? |
| fragen | to ask | Ich frage den Lehrer. |
| spielen | to play | Die Kinder spielen im Garten. |
| kochen | to cook | Meine Mutter kocht gut. |
| brauchen | to need | Ich brauche Hilfe. |
| suchen | to search | Wir suchen ein Restaurant. |
| zeigen | to show | Zeig mir das Bild. |
| glauben | to believe | Ich glaube dir. |
| lieben | to love | Sie liebt Schokolade. |
| tanzen | to dance | Tanzt du gern? |

## Stems Ending in -t, -d, -n, or -m (with preceding consonant)

When the stem ends in -t, -d, or consonant cluster with -n/-m, add an -e before the -st and -t endings for pronunciation:

**ARBEITEN (to work): Stem = arbeit-**
ich arbeite, du arbeit**e**st, er arbeit**e**t, wir arbeiten, ihr arbeit**e**t, sie arbeiten

Other verbs like this: finden (to find), warten (to wait), öffnen (to open), rechnen (to calculate), atmen (to breathe), zeichnen (to draw)

## Stems Ending in -s, -ß, -z, or -x

The du form loses the -s from -st (the stem already has a sibilant):

**REISEN (to travel): Stem = reis-**
du reist (NOT "du reisst")

Also: sitzen (du sitzt), heizen (du heizt), tanzen (du tanzt)

## The V2 Rule (Verb in Second Position)

In German main clauses, the conjugated verb MUST be in the second position. This is the most important word order rule:

| Position 1 | Position 2 (VERB) | Position 3+ |
|-----------|-------------------|-------------|
| Ich | lerne | Deutsch. |
| Heute | lerne | ich Deutsch. |
| Am Montag | spielen | wir Fußball. |
| Deutsch | lerne | ich jeden Tag. |

When something other than the subject is in first position, the subject moves to position 3 (subject-verb inversion). The verb ALWAYS stays in position 2.

## Negation

Place "nicht" after the verb (or at the end of the sentence) to negate:
- Ich spiele nicht. (I don't play.)
- Er kommt heute nicht. (He's not coming today.)
- Wir wohnen nicht in Berlin. (We don't live in Berlin.)

Use "kein" (no/not a) instead of "nicht ein":
- Ich habe kein Auto. (I don't have a car.)
- Ich habe keine Zeit. (I don't have time.)

## Practice

Conjugate spielen, lernen, and arbeiten for all persons. Then write eight sentences about your daily life using different regular verbs.

# Important Irregular Verbs and Stem-Changing Verbs

## SEIN (to be) — Completely Irregular

| Person | Form |
|--------|------|
| ich | bin |
| du | bist |
| er/sie/es | ist |
| wir | sind |
| ihr | seid |
| sie/Sie | sind |

**Uses:** identity, nationality, profession, description, location (with adjectives).
- Ich bin Student. (I am a student.)
- Sie ist groß. (She is tall.)
- Wir sind müde. (We are tired.)
- Wo bist du? (Where are you?)

## HABEN (to have)

| Person | Form |
|--------|------|
| ich | habe |
| du | hast |
| er/sie/es | hat |
| wir | haben |
| ihr | habt |
| sie/Sie | haben |

**Uses:** possession, auxiliary for past tense, expressions.
- Ich habe zwei Katzen. (I have two cats.)
- Hast du Zeit? (Do you have time?)
- Er hat Hunger. (He is hungry.)
- Sie hat Recht. (She is right.)

## WERDEN (to become) — Also Used for Future Tense

| Person | Form |
|--------|------|
| ich | werde |
| du | wirst |
| er/sie/es | wird |
| wir | werden |
| ihr | werdet |
| sie/Sie | werden |

- Er wird Arzt. (He is becoming a doctor.)
- Es wird kalt. (It's getting cold.)

## WISSEN (to know — facts)

| Person | Form |
|--------|------|
| ich | weiß |
| du | weißt |
| er/sie/es | weiß |
| wir | wissen |
| ihr | wisst |
| sie/Sie | wissen |

- Ich weiß es nicht. (I don't know.)
- Weißt du, wo er ist? (Do you know where he is?)

**Wissen vs. Kennen:** Wissen = to know facts/information. Kennen = to know/be familiar with people, places, things.
- Ich weiß, dass er aus Berlin kommt. (I know that he comes from Berlin.)
- Ich kenne Berlin gut. (I know Berlin well.)
- Kennst du meinen Bruder? (Do you know my brother?)

## Stem-Changing Verbs

Many common German verbs change their stem vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms:

**e → i:**
| Infinitive | du | er/sie/es | Meaning |
|-----------|-----|-----------|---------|
| sprechen | sprichst | spricht | to speak |
| essen | isst | isst | to eat |
| geben | gibst | gibt | to give |
| helfen | hilfst | hilft | to help |
| nehmen | nimmst | nimmt | to take |
| treffen | triffst | trifft | to meet |
| vergessen | vergisst | vergisst | to forget |

**e → ie:**
| Infinitive | du | er/sie/es | Meaning |
|-----------|-----|-----------|---------|
| lesen | liest | liest | to read |
| sehen | siehst | sieht | to see |
| empfehlen | empfiehlst | empfiehlt | to recommend |

**a → ä:**
| Infinitive | du | er/sie/es | Meaning |
|-----------|-----|-----------|---------|
| fahren | fährst | fährt | to drive/go |
| schlafen | schläfst | schläft | to sleep |
| tragen | trägst | trägt | to carry/wear |
| fallen | fällst | fällt | to fall |
| laufen | läufst | läuft | to run/walk |
| waschen | wäschst | wäscht | to wash |

**au → äu:**
| laufen | läufst | läuft | to run |

**Important:** The stem change only occurs in du and er/sie/es forms. All other forms use the regular stem.

- Er spricht Deutsch. (He speaks German.)
- Du liest ein Buch. (You're reading a book.)
- Sie fährt nach Hamburg. (She drives to Hamburg.)
- But: Wir sprechen Englisch. (We speak English. — no change)

Conjugate sein, haben, sprechen, and fahren for all persons. Write sentences using stem-changing verbs: Er liest gern. Sie fährt mit dem Bus. Du sprichst gut Deutsch.

# Modal Verbs

## The Six Modal Verbs

Modal verbs express ability, permission, obligation, desire, or preference. They are used with an infinitive, which goes to the END of the sentence.

## Conjugation

Modal verbs share a pattern: the ich and er/sie/es forms are identical, and most change their vowel in singular forms.

| | können (can) | müssen (must) | wollen (want) | sollen (should) | dürfen (may) | mögen (like) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | kann | muss | will | soll | darf | mag |
| du | kannst | musst | willst | sollst | darfst | magst |
| er/sie/es | kann | muss | will | soll | darf | mag |
| wir | können | müssen | wollen | sollen | dürfen | mögen |
| ihr | könnt | müsst | wollt | sollt | dürft | mögt |
| sie/Sie | können | müssen | wollen | sollen | dürfen | mögen |

## Usage and Examples

**KÖNNEN (can, to be able to):**
- Ich kann Deutsch sprechen. (I can speak German.)
- Kannst du schwimmen? (Can you swim?)
- Er kann gut kochen. (He can cook well.)

**MÜSSEN (must, to have to):**
- Ich muss heute arbeiten. (I must work today.)
- Wir müssen jetzt gehen. (We have to go now.)
- Du musst mehr lernen. (You have to study more.)
- **"Must not" ≠ "muss nicht"!** "Ich muss nicht" = I don't have to. "I must not" = Ich darf nicht.

**WOLLEN (to want):**
- Ich will ins Kino gehen. (I want to go to the movies.)
- Was willst du essen? (What do you want to eat?)
- Wir wollen nach Deutschland reisen. (We want to travel to Germany.)

**SOLLEN (should, to be supposed to):**
- Du sollst mehr Wasser trinken. (You should drink more water.)
- Was soll ich machen? (What should I do?)
- Er soll um acht Uhr kommen. (He is supposed to come at eight.)

**DÜRFEN (may, to be allowed to):**
- Darf ich hier sitzen? (May I sit here?)
- Hier darf man nicht rauchen. (One may not smoke here.)
- Kinder dürfen nicht Alkohol trinken. (Children may not drink alcohol.)

**MÖGEN (to like) — and MÖCHTEN (would like):**
- Ich mag Schokolade. (I like chocolate.)
- Sie mag keine Spinnen. (She doesn't like spiders.)
- **Möchten** (would like) is the subjunctive of mögen and is extremely common:
  ich möchte, du möchtest, er möchte, wir möchten, ihr möchtet, sie möchten
- Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. (I would like a coffee, please.)
- Möchten Sie bestellen? (Would you like to order?)

## Word Order with Modal Verbs

The modal verb is conjugated and goes in position 2. The main verb stays in the infinitive and goes to the END of the sentence:

| Position 1 | Position 2 (Modal) | Middle | End (Infinitive) |
|-----------|-------------------|--------|------------------|
| Ich | kann | gut Deutsch | sprechen. |
| Er | muss | heute | arbeiten. |
| Wir | wollen | morgen ins Kino | gehen. |
| Du | darfst | hier nicht | rauchen. |

**In questions:** Kannst du Deutsch sprechen? (Can you speak German?)
**With negation:** Ich kann nicht schwimmen. (I can't swim.) — "nicht" goes before the infinitive.

3. Was willst du am Wochenende machen?
4. Was sollst du öfter machen?

# Perfekt: The Conversational Past Tense

## What Is the Perfekt?

The Perfekt is the most common past tense in spoken German. It is used for completed actions in everyday conversation, similar to both "I have done" and "I did" in English. Written German and formal narratives tend to use the Präteritum (simple past), but in speech, the Perfekt dominates.

## Formation

Perfekt = **subject + auxiliary (haben or sein) + past participle (at the end)**

## Past Participles of Regular (Weak) Verbs

Regular verbs form their past participle with: **ge- + stem + -t**

| Infinitive | Past Participle | Example |
|-----------|----------------|---------|
| machen | gemacht | Ich habe es gemacht. (I did it.) |
| spielen | gespielt | Wir haben Fußball gespielt. (We played soccer.) |
| kaufen | gekauft | Sie hat ein Buch gekauft. (She bought a book.) |
| lernen | gelernt | Ich habe Deutsch gelernt. (I learned German.) |
| kochen | gekocht | Er hat das Essen gekocht. (He cooked the food.) |

## Using HABEN (most verbs)

Most verbs form the Perfekt with haben:
- Ich **habe** ein Buch **gelesen**. (I read a book.)
- Er **hat** das Essen **gekocht**. (He cooked the food.)
- Wir **haben** Musik **gehört**. (We listened to music.)

## Using SEIN (movement and change of state)

Verbs that express a change of location or change of state use sein:

| Infinitive | Past Participle | Example |
|-----------|----------------|---------|
| gehen | gegangen | Ich bin nach Hause gegangen. (I went home.) |
| kommen | gekommen | Er ist gestern gekommen. (He came yesterday.) |
| fahren | gefahren | Wir sind nach Berlin gefahren. (We drove to Berlin.) |
| fliegen | geflogen | Sie ist nach Japan geflogen. (She flew to Japan.) |
| laufen | gelaufen | Ich bin zur Schule gelaufen. (I walked to school.) |
| schwimmen | geschwommen | Er ist im See geschwommen. (He swam in the lake.) |
| bleiben | geblieben | Wir sind zu Hause geblieben. (We stayed home.) |
| sein | gewesen | Ich bin in Deutschland gewesen. (I have been in Germany.) |
| werden | geworden | Es ist kalt geworden. (It got cold.) |
| sterben | gestorben | Er ist gestorben. (He died.) |
| aufwachen | aufgewacht | Ich bin um sechs aufgewacht. (I woke up at six.) |

- Movement from A to B: gehen, kommen, fahren, fliegen, reisen, laufen
- Change of state: werden, sterben, wachsen (grow), einschlafen, aufwachen

The past participle always goes to the END of the sentence:
- Ich **habe** gestern ein Buch **gekauft**. (I bought a book yesterday.)
- **Hast** du schon **gegessen**? (Have you eaten already?)
- Er **ist** nach Berlin **gefahren**. (He drove to Berlin.)
- Was **hast** du am Wochenende **gemacht**? (What did you do on the weekend?)

Write about what you did last weekend using at least ten Perfekt verbs, mixing haben and sein: Am Samstag bin ich aufgestanden und habe gefrühstückt. Dann bin ich ins Kino gegangen. Ich habe einen Film gesehen...

**Practice and Application**

Mastering German requires consistent engagement with the language across all four skills: reading, writing, listening, and speaking. German has a reputation among English speakers as being difficult, but this reputation is somewhat misleading. While German grammar is more complex than English in certain respects (three genders, four cases, complex word order rules, and extensive verb conjugation), the two languages share Germanic roots that provide a substantial foundation of cognate vocabulary and structural similarities. English speakers who approach German systematically can leverage these similarities while focusing their efforts on the areas of genuine difference.

Vocabulary acquisition is supported by the systematic nature of German word formation. German is famous for its compound nouns (Zusammensetzungen), which combine two or more words into a single, often lengthy word whose meaning can usually be deduced from its components. For example, Handschuh (glove) literally means hand-shoe, Staubsauger (vacuum cleaner) means dust-sucker, and Krankenversicherung (health insurance) means sick-insurance. Understanding the component-building principle allows learners to decode unfamiliar compound words and to recognize the semantic relationships between related words. German also uses a highly productive system of prefixes and suffixes to create new words from existing roots, further expanding the learner's ability to deduce meaning from word structure.

Pronunciation in German is generally more regular and predictable than in English. Once the sound values of individual letters and letter combinations are learned, most words can be pronounced correctly on sight, unlike English where spelling-to-pronunciation correspondence is notoriously inconsistent. Key pronunciation features that require specific attention from English speakers include the umlauted vowels (ae, oe, ue), the ch sound (which has two variants: the palatal ich-Laut after front vowels and consonants, and the velar ach-Laut after back vowels), the r sound (typically a uvular fricative or trill, quite different from the English r), and the distinction between long and short vowels (which is phonemic in German, meaning it changes word meaning: Staat/state versus Stadt/city).

The case system (Nominativ, Akkusativ, Dativ, Genitiv) is often cited as the most challenging aspect of German grammar for English speakers. Cases indicate the grammatical function of nouns and pronouns in a sentence (subject, direct object, indirect object, possession), and they affect the forms of articles, adjectives, and pronouns. English retains vestiges of a case system in pronouns (I/me/my, he/him/his, who/whom/whose), but German applies case distinctions systematically across all nouns and their modifiers. The key to mastering cases is understanding their functional logic rather than simply memorizing tables: the nominative identifies the subject (who or what does the action), the accusative identifies the direct object (who or what receives the action), the dative identifies the indirect object (to or for whom), and the genitive indicates possession (whose). Many prepositions require specific cases, and the two-way prepositions (Wechselpraepositionen: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, ueber, unter, vor, zwischen) take either accusative (indicating motion toward) or dative (indicating location at), depending on the meaning intended.

These regions share a common language but have distinct cultural identities, customs, dialects, and culinary traditions. Understanding these cultural dimensions enhances language learning by providing authentic contexts for vocabulary and grammar, motivating continued study through cultural interest, and developing intercultural competence that is valuable in personal and professional contexts.

German-speaking countries have made enormous contributions to world culture in philosophy (Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Wittgenstein, Heidegger), music (Bach, Beethoven, Mozart, Wagner, Strauss, Schoenberg), literature (Goethe, Schiller, Kafka, Mann, Hesse, Rilke), science (Einstein, Heisenberg, Planck, Koch, Roentgen), and psychology (Freud, Jung). Engaging with these cultural contributions in their original language provides deeper understanding and appreciation than translation alone can offer.

# Irregular Past Participles and Special Cases

## Strong (Irregular) Verb Past Participles

Strong verbs form their past participle with: **ge- + changed stem + -en**

These stem changes must be memorized. Here are the most common:

| Infinitive | Past Participle | Meaning |
|-----------|----------------|---------|
| sein | gewesen | to be |
| haben | gehabt | to have |
| werden | geworden | to become |
| essen | gegessen | to eat |
| trinken | getrunken | to drink |
| schreiben | geschrieben | to write |
| lesen | gelesen | to read |
| sprechen | gesprochen | to speak |
| nehmen | genommen | to take |
| geben | gegeben | to give |
| sehen | gesehen | to see |
| finden | gefunden | to find |
| helfen | geholfen | to help |
| tragen | getragen | to carry/wear |
| waschen | gewaschen | to wash |
| singen | gesungen | to sing |
| beginnen | begonnen | to begin |
| gewinnen | gewonnen | to win |
| liegen | gelegen | to lie/be situated |
| sitzen | gesessen | to sit |
| stehen | gestanden | to stand |
| rufen | gerufen | to call |
| schließen | geschlossen | to close |
| ziehen | gezogen | to pull/move |
| tun | getan | to do |

## Inseparable Prefix Verbs — No ge-!

Verbs with inseparable prefixes (be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer-) do NOT add ge- in the past participle:

| Infinitive | Past Participle | Meaning |
|-----------|----------------|---------|
| verstehen | verstanden | to understand |
| bekommen | bekommen | to receive/get |
| erzählen | erzählt | to tell/narrate |
| empfehlen | empfohlen | to recommend |
| entscheiden | entschieden | to decide |
| vergessen | vergessen | to forget |
| besuchen | besucht | to visit |
| erklären | erklärt | to explain |
| bezahlen | bezahlt | to pay |
| gehören | gehört | to belong |
| zerbrechen | zerbrochen | to break (into pieces) |
| misslingen | misslungen | to fail |

**Examples:**
- Ich habe den Film nicht verstanden. (I didn't understand the movie.)
- Sie hat einen Brief bekommen. (She received a letter.)
- Er hat die Geschichte erzählt. (He told the story.)
- Hast du das nicht vergessen? (Didn't you forget that?)

## Separable Prefix Verbs — ge- Goes in the Middle!

Separable prefix verbs (ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, vor-, zu-, zurück-, etc.) insert ge- BETWEEN the prefix and the stem:

| Infinitive | Past Participle | Meaning |
|-----------|----------------|---------|
| aufstehen | aufgestanden | to get up |
| anfangen | angefangen | to begin |
| einkaufen | eingekauft | to shop |
| mitkommen | mitgekommen | to come along |
| zurückkommen | zurückgekommen | to come back |
| aufmachen | aufgemacht | to open |
| zumachen | zugemacht | to close |
| anrufen | angerufen | to call (phone) |
| aufhören | aufgehört | to stop |
| ausgehen | ausgegangen | to go out |
| einladen | eingeladen | to invite |
| umziehen | umgezogen | to move (house) |

**Examples:**
- Ich bin um sechs Uhr aufgestanden. (I got up at six.)
- Wir haben im Supermarkt eingekauft. (We shopped at the supermarket.)
- Er hat mich zum Essen eingeladen. (He invited me to dinner.)
- Hast du schon angerufen? (Have you called already?)

## Verbs Ending in -ieren — No ge-!

Verbs borrowed from French/Latin ending in -ieren do not add ge-:

| Infinitive | Past Participle | Meaning |
|-----------|----------------|---------|
| studieren | studiert | to study (at university) |

# Präteritum (Simple Past) and Future Tense

## Präteritum: When to Use It

The Präteritum (simple past / narrative past) is used mainly in written German — novels, news, formal reports — and in everyday speech for a few high-frequency verbs (sein, haben, modal verbs). For most other verbs, spoken German uses the Perfekt.

## Sein and Haben in the Präteritum

These are the most important Präteritum forms because they are used constantly in speech:

**SEIN (was/were):**
| Person | Form |
|--------|------|
| ich | war |
| du | warst |
| er/sie/es | war |
| wir | waren |
| ihr | wart |
| sie/Sie | waren |

**HABEN (had):**
| Person | Form |
|--------|------|
| ich | hatte |
| du | hattest |
| er/sie/es | hatte |
| wir | hatten |
| ihr | hattet |
| sie/Sie | hatten |

**Examples:**
- Ich war gestern in Berlin. (I was in Berlin yesterday.) — NOT "Ich bin gewesen"
- Wir hatten viel Spaß. (We had a lot of fun.) — NOT "Wir haben gehabt"
- Es war schönes Wetter. (The weather was nice.)
- Hattest du Zeit? (Did you have time?)

## Regular Verbs in the Präteritum

Regular (weak) verbs add -te to the stem:

**MACHEN (to do/make): mach-**
ich machte, du machtest, er machte, wir machten, ihr machtet, sie machten

**SPIELEN: spiel-**
ich spielte, du spieltest, er spielte, wir spielten, ihr spieltet, sie spielten

## Strong (Irregular) Verbs in the Präteritum

Strong verbs change their stem vowel:

| Infinitive | Präteritum (ich/er) | Meaning |
|-----------|---------------------|---------|
| gehen | ging | to go |
| kommen | kam | to come |
| fahren | fuhr | to drive |
| schreiben | schrieb | to write |
| sprechen | sprach | to speak |
| sehen | sah | to see |
| geben | gab | to give |
| nehmen | nahm | to take |
| finden | fand | to find |
| stehen | stand | to stand |
| lesen | las | to read |
| trinken | trank | to drink |
| essen | aß | to eat |
| singen | sang | to sing |
| rufen | rief | to call |
| schließen | schloss | to close |
| werden | wurde | to become |

**Endings for strong verbs:** ich -(no ending), du -st, er -(no ending), wir -en, ihr -t, sie -en

Example: gehen → ich ging, du gingst, er ging, wir gingen, ihr gingt, sie gingen

## Modal Verbs in the Präteritum

Modal verbs in the Präteritum are very common in speech:

| Infinitive | Präteritum (ich) |
|-----------|-----------------|
| können | konnte |
| müssen | musste |
| wollen | wollte |
| sollen | sollte |
| dürfen | durfte |
| mögen | mochte |

- Ich konnte nicht kommen. (I couldn't come.)
- Er musste arbeiten. (He had to work.)
- Sie wollte nach Hause gehen. (She wanted to go home.)

## Das Futur I (Future Tense)

The future tense uses **werden + infinitive (at the end)**:

| Person | werden | Example |
|--------|--------|---------|
| ich | werde | Ich werde morgen kommen. |
| du | wirst | Du wirst es schaffen. |
| er/sie/es | wird | Er wird Arzt werden. |
| wir | werden | Wir werden sehen. |
| ihr | werdet | Ihr werdet es verstehen. |
| sie/Sie | werden | Sie werden gewinnen. |

**Uses:**
1. Future events: Ich werde morgen kommen. (I will come tomorrow.)
2. Predictions: Das Wetter wird besser sein. (The weather will be better.)
3. Intentions: Ich werde mehr lernen. (I will study more.)
4. Probability/assumption: Er wird wohl krank sein. (He's probably sick.)

**Note:** In everyday German, the present tense + a time word often replaces the future: Ich komme morgen. (I'm coming tomorrow.) is more natural than Ich werde morgen kommen.

## Practice

Rewrite these present-tense sentences in both Perfekt and Präteritum:
1. Ich gehe in die Schule. → Ich bin...gegangen / Ich ging...
2. Er liest ein Buch. → Er hat...gelesen / Er las...
Write five sentences about what you will do next week using the future tense.

# The Four German Cases: Overview

## Why Cases Matter

German uses four grammatical cases to show the function of nouns in a sentence. Cases change the articles, adjective endings, and sometimes the nouns themselves. Understanding cases is the single most important step toward German fluency.

## The Four Cases

| Case | Function | Question | Example |
|------|----------|----------|---------|
| Nominativ | Subject (who/what does it) | Wer? Was? | **Der Mann** liest. (The man reads.) |
| Akkusativ | Direct object (whom/what receives it) | Wen? Was? | Ich sehe **den Mann**. (I see the man.) |
| Dativ | Indirect object (to/for whom) | Wem? | Ich gebe **dem Mann** ein Buch. (I give the man a book.) |
| Genitiv | Possession (whose) | Wessen? | Das Auto **des Mannes**. (The man's car.) |

## Article Changes by Case

**Definite articles (der/die/das):**

| Case | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter | Plural |
|------|-----------|----------|--------|--------|
| Nominativ | der | die | das | die |
| Akkusativ | **den** | die | das | die |
| Dativ | **dem** | **der** | **dem** | **den** (+n on noun) |
| Genitiv | **des** (+s/es on noun) | **der** | **des** (+s/es on noun) | **der** |

**Indefinite articles (ein/eine):**

| Case | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
|------|-----------|----------|--------|
| Nominativ | ein | eine | ein |
| Akkusativ | **einen** | eine | ein |
| Dativ | **einem** | **einer** | **einem** |
| Genitiv | **eines** (+s/es) | **einer** | **eines** (+s/es) |

## Nominativ (Subject)

The subject of the sentence — who or what performs the action:
- **Der Hund** schläft. (The dog sleeps.)
- **Die Frau** liest ein Buch. (The woman reads a book.)
- **Das Kind** spielt im Garten. (The child plays in the garden.)

Also used after sein (to be), werden (to become), bleiben (to remain):
- Er ist **ein guter Lehrer**. (He is a good teacher.)

## Akkusativ (Direct Object)

The direct object — who or what receives the action:
- Ich sehe **den Mann**. (I see the man.)
- Er kauft **eine Jacke**. (He buys a jacket.)
- Wir lesen **das Buch**. (We read the book.)

**Only the masculine article changes:** der → den, ein → einen. Feminine, neuter, and plural stay the same.

## Dativ (Indirect Object)

The indirect object — to whom or for whom:
- Ich gebe **dem Kind** ein Geschenk. (I give the child a gift.)
- Er hilft **der Frau**. (He helps the woman.)
- Ich schreibe **meinem Freund** einen Brief. (I write my friend a letter.)

**All articles change in the dative.** Plural nouns add -n if they don't already end in -n: die Kinder → den Kindern, die Frauen → den Frauen (already -n).

## Genitiv (Possession)

Shows possession or "of":
- Das Auto **des Mannes**. (The man's car / The car of the man.)
- Die Tasche **der Frau**. (The woman's bag.)
- Der Name **des Kindes**. (The child's name.)

Masculine and neuter nouns add **-(e)s** in the genitive: des Mannes, des Buches, des Kindes.

## Practice

Identify the case of the underlined words:
1. **Der Lehrer** gibt **dem Schüler** **ein Buch**. (Nom, Dat, Akk)
2. Ich sehe **den Hund** **des Nachbarn**. (Akk, Gen)
3. **Die Mutter** hilft **der Tochter**. (Nom, Dat)

# Accusative and Dative: Prepositions and Two-Way Prepositions

## Accusative Prepositions

These prepositions ALWAYS take the accusative case:

**Memory aid: DOGFU** — durch, ohne, gegen, für, um

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|------------|---------|---------|
| durch | through | Wir gehen durch **den** Park. (through the park) |
| ohne | without | Ich gehe ohne **meinen** Bruder. (without my brother) |
| gegen | against | Er spielt gegen **den** Weltmeister. (against the champion) |
| für | for | Das ist für **dich**. (That's for you.) |
| um | around/at (time) | Wir sitzen um **den** Tisch. (around the table) |

**Examples:**
- Ich kaufe ein Geschenk für **meine Mutter** (Akk). (I buy a gift for my mother.)
- Er läuft durch **die Stadt** (Akk). (He runs through the city.)
- Ohne **einen Regenschirm** (Akk) gehe ich nicht raus. (I won't go out without an umbrella.)

## Dative Prepositions

These prepositions ALWAYS take the dative case:

**Memory aid: AUS-BEI-MIT-NACH-SEIT-VON-ZU (said rhythmically)**

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|------------|---------|---------|
| aus | out of / from | Ich komme aus **der** Schweiz. (from Switzerland) |
| bei | at / near / at someone's | Ich wohne bei **meinen** Eltern. (at my parents') |
| mit | with | Ich fahre mit **dem** Bus. (by bus) |
| nach | after / to (countries/cities) | Nach **dem** Essen gehen wir. (After the meal we go.) |
| seit | since / for (time) | Seit **einem** Jahr lerne ich Deutsch. (For a year I've been learning.) |
| von | from / of | Das Buch ist von **meinem** Freund. (The book is from my friend.) |
| zu | to | Ich gehe zu **meiner** Großmutter. (I go to my grandmother's.) |
| gegenüber | across from | Gegenüber **dem** Bahnhof. (Across from the station.) |
| außer | except | Alle außer **mir**. (Everyone except me.) |

**Common contractions:**
- bei + dem = beim: Ich bin beim Arzt. (I'm at the doctor's.)
- von + dem = vom: Ich komme vom Bahnhof. (I come from the station.)
- zu + dem = zum: Ich gehe zum Supermarkt. (I go to the supermarket.)
- zu + der = zur: Ich gehe zur Schule. (I go to school.)

## Two-Way Prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen)

These nine prepositions take EITHER accusative OR dative depending on meaning:

| Preposition | Meaning |
|------------|---------|
| in | in / into |
| an | at / on (vertical) |
| auf | on (horizontal) |
| über | over / above |
| unter | under |
| vor | in front of / before |
| hinter | behind |
| neben | next to |
| zwischen | between |

**The rule:**
- **ACCUSATIVE** = motion/direction (Wohin? — Where to?) — action is moving toward something
- **DATIVE** = location/position (Wo? — Where?) — action is staying in one place

| Akkusativ (Wohin? — movement) | Dativ (Wo? — location) |
|------------------------------|----------------------|
| Ich gehe **in die** Schule. (I go INTO school.) | Ich bin **in der** Schule. (I am IN school.) |
| Er legt das Buch **auf den** Tisch. (He puts the book ON the table.) | Das Buch liegt **auf dem** Tisch. (The book is ON the table.) |
| Sie hängt das Bild **an die** Wand. (She hangs the picture ON the wall.) | Das Bild hängt **an der** Wand. (The picture hangs ON the wall.) |

**Common contractions:**
- in + dem = im: Ich bin im Kino. (I'm at the movies.)
- in + das = ins: Ich gehe ins Kino. (I go to the movies.)
- an + dem = am: Am Montag. (On Monday.)
- an + das = ans: Er geht ans Fenster. (He goes to the window.)

## Verb Pairs for Two-Way Prepositions

German has pairs of verbs where one shows motion (Akkusativ) and the other shows position (Dativ):

| Motion (Akk) | Position (Dat) | English |
|-------------|---------------|---------|
| legen (to lay) | liegen (to lie) | put flat / be lying |
| stellen (to place upright) | stehen (to stand) | put standing / be standing |
| setzen (to set/seat) | sitzen (to sit) | put sitting / be sitting |
| hängen (to hang — transitive) | hängen (to hang — intransitive) | hang up / be hanging |

## Practice

Choose Akkusativ or Dativ:
1. Ich bin in ___ Schule. (der — Dativ, location)
2. Ich gehe in ___ Schule. (die — Akkusativ, movement)
3. Das Bild hängt an ___ Wand. (der — Dativ, location)
4. Sie fährt mit ___ Bus. (dem — Dativ, always dative after mit)

# Genitive Case and Adjective Endings

## The Genitive Case

The genitive shows possession and is equivalent to "'s" or "of" in English.

**Article changes:**

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter | Plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominativ | der | die | das | die |
| Genitiv | **des** | **der** | **des** | **der** |

**Masculine and neuter nouns add -(e)s:**
- Das Buch **des Lehrers** (The teacher's book)
- Der Name **des Kindes** (The child's name)
- Die Farbe **des Autos** (The color of the car)

One-syllable nouns often add -es: des Mannes, des Hundes, des Buches.
Multi-syllable nouns usually add just -s: des Lehrers, des Computers, des Mädchens.

**Feminine and plural nouns do not change:**
- Die Tasche **der Frau** (The woman's bag)
- Das Spielzeug **der Kinder** (The children's toy)

## Genitive Prepositions

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|------------|---------|---------|
| während | during | Während **des Sommers** reise ich. (During summer I travel.) |
| wegen | because of | Wegen **des Regens** bleiben wir zu Hause. (Because of the rain we stay home.) |
| trotz | despite | Trotz **des schlechten Wetters** gehen wir spazieren. (Despite the bad weather we go for a walk.) |
| statt / anstatt | instead of | Statt **eines Kuchens** kaufe ich Obst. (Instead of a cake I buy fruit.) |
| außerhalb | outside of | Außerhalb **der Stadt**. (Outside the city.) |
| innerhalb | inside of / within | Innerhalb **eines Jahres**. (Within a year.) |

**Note:** In informal speech, wegen and trotz are increasingly used with the dative (wegen dem Regen), but the genitive remains correct in formal German.

## Adjective Endings (Adjektivdeklination)

This is one of the most complex aspects of German grammar. Adjective endings depend on three factors: (1) the case, (2) the gender/number, and (3) what article (if any) precedes the adjective.

**Type 1: After definite articles (der, die, das, etc.)**

All endings are -e or -en:

| Case | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter | Plural |
|------|-----------|----------|--------|--------|
| Nom | der alt**e** Mann | die alt**e** Frau | das alt**e** Kind | die alt**en** Kinder |
| Akk | den alt**en** Mann | die alt**e** Frau | das alt**e** Kind | die alt**en** Kinder |
| Dat | dem alt**en** Mann | der alt**en** Frau | dem alt**en** Kind | den alt**en** Kindern |
| Gen | des alt**en** Mannes | der alt**en** Frau | des alt**en** Kindes | der alt**en** Kinder |

**Rule:** Nominative masculine, feminine, neuter singular → -e. Everything else → -en.

**Type 2: After indefinite articles (ein, eine, kein, mein, etc.)**

| Case | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter | Plural (keine) |
|------|-----------|----------|--------|--------|
| Nom | ein alt**er** Mann | eine alt**e** Frau | ein alt**es** Kind | keine alt**en** Kinder |
| Akk | einen alt**en** Mann | eine alt**e** Frau | ein alt**es** Kind | keine alt**en** Kinder |
| Dat | einem alt**en** Mann | einer alt**en** Frau | einem alt**en** Kind | keinen alt**en** Kindern |
| Gen | eines alt**en** Mannes | einer alt**en** Frau | eines alt**en** Kindes | keiner alt**en** Kinder |

**Rule:** Where ein has NO ending (ein_ Mann, ein_ Kind), the adjective shows the gender with a strong ending (-er for masc, -es for neuter). Elsewhere → same as definite article pattern.

**Type 3: No article (rare, mostly plural or with uncountable nouns)**

| Case | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter | Plural |
|------|-----------|----------|--------|--------|
| Nom | alt**er** Wein | kalt**e** Milch | frisch**es** Brot | alt**e** Häuser |
| Akk | alt**en** Wein | kalt**e** Milch | frisch**es** Brot | alt**e** Häuser |

The adjective itself carries the strong ending to show gender/case.

## Simplified Approach

If this seems overwhelming, focus on the most common situations:
1. After der/die/das → almost always -en (except Nom. sing. → -e)
2. After ein/eine → the adjective fills in the gender info that ein doesn't show
3. Practice with real sentences rather than memorizing tables

## Practice

Fill in the adjective ending:
1. der groß___ Hund (der große Hund — Nom. masc.)
2. ein gut___ Buch (ein gutes Buch — Nom. neuter)
3. mit dem alt___ Auto (mit dem alten Auto — Dat. neuter)
4. die schön___ Blumen (die schönen Blumen — Nom. plural)
5. für einen jung___ Mann (für einen jungen Mann — Akk. masc.)

# German Sentence Structure: Main and Subordinate Clauses

## The V2 Rule in Main Clauses

The most fundamental rule of German word order: in a main clause (Hauptsatz), the conjugated verb is ALWAYS in the SECOND position.

| Position 1 | Position 2 (VERB) | Remaining elements |
|-----------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Ich | gehe | heute in die Schule. |
| Heute | gehe | ich in die Schule. |
| In die Schule | gehe | ich heute. |
| Am Montag | spielen | wir Fußball. |

**Position 1 can be occupied by:**
- The subject: **Ich** lerne Deutsch.
- A time expression: **Morgen** fahre ich nach Berlin.
- An object: **Das Buch** habe ich gelesen.
- An adverb: **Leider** kann ich nicht kommen.
- A subordinate clause: **Wenn es regnet**, bleibe ich zu Hause.

When something other than the subject fills Position 1, the subject moves to Position 3 (subject-verb inversion). The verb STAYS in Position 2.

## Subordinate Clauses: Verb to the End

In subordinate clauses (Nebensätze), the conjugated verb goes to the VERY END. These clauses are introduced by subordinating conjunctions:

**Common subordinating conjunctions:**

| Conjunction | Meaning | Example |
|------------|---------|---------|
| dass | that | Ich weiß, **dass er Deutsch spricht**. |
| weil | because | Ich lerne Deutsch, **weil es interessant ist**. |
| wenn | if / when (present/future) | **Wenn es regnet**, bleibe ich zu Hause. |
| als | when (past, single event) | **Als ich jung war**, spielte ich viel. |
| obwohl | although | **Obwohl er müde ist**, arbeitet er. |
| bevor | before | **Bevor ich esse**, wasche ich mir die Hände. |
| nachdem | after | **Nachdem er gegessen hatte**, ging er. |
| während | while | **Während ich lese**, hört er Musik. |
| bis | until | Warte, **bis ich komme**. |
| damit | so that | Ich lerne, **damit ich gute Noten bekomme**. |
| ob | whether/if | Ich weiß nicht, **ob er kommt**. |
| seit/seitdem | since (time) | **Seitdem ich hier wohne**, bin ich glücklich. |

**Structure:** Main clause + , + conjunction + subject + ... + **VERB AT END**
- Ich lerne Deutsch, **weil ich nach Deutschland reisen will**.
  (I learn German because I want to travel to Germany.)
  Notice: "will" (the conjugated modal) goes to the end, and "reisen" (the infinitive) goes right before it.

**When the subordinate clause comes FIRST, the main clause verb comes immediately after the comma (Position 2 of the overall sentence):**
- Weil ich müde **bin**, **gehe** ich ins Bett.
  (Because I am tired, I go to bed.)

## Double Infinitive in Subordinate Clauses

When a modal verb is used in the Perfekt within a subordinate clause, the conjugated auxiliary goes BEFORE the double infinitive:
- ..., weil er hat kommen **können**. → ..., weil er **hat** kommen **können**.
  (Both forms are used, but the second is more standard in writing.)

Combine these sentences using the conjunction in parentheses:
1. Ich bleibe zu Hause. Es regnet. (weil) → Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil es regnet.
2. Er spricht gut Deutsch. Er hat in Deutschland gewohnt. (weil) → Er spricht gut Deutsch, weil er in Deutschland gewohnt hat.
3. Ich weiß nicht. Er kommt morgen. (ob) → Ich weiß nicht, ob er morgen kommt.

# Coordinating Conjunctions, Questions, and Relative Clauses

## Coordinating Conjunctions (ADUSO)

Unlike subordinating conjunctions, coordinating conjunctions do NOT change the word order. The verb stays in Position 2 of its clause.

**ADUSO:** aber, denn, und, sondern, oder

| Conjunction | Meaning | Example |
|------------|---------|---------|
| aber | but | Ich bin müde, **aber** ich muss arbeiten. |
| denn | because/for | Er bleibt zu Hause, **denn** er ist krank. |
| und | and | Ich lerne Deutsch **und** er lernt Französisch. |
| sondern | but rather (after negation) | Er ist nicht dumm, **sondern** faul. |
| oder | or | Kommst du mit **oder** bleibst du hier? |

**Denn vs. Weil:** Both mean "because," but denn is a coordinating conjunction (normal word order) and weil is subordinating (verb to end):
- Er bleibt zu Hause, **denn** er **ist** krank. (V2 order)
- Er bleibt zu Hause, **weil** er krank **ist**. (verb at end)

**Sondern vs. Aber:** Use "sondern" only after a negation when you want to correct with "but rather/instead":
- Das ist nicht rot, **sondern** blau. (That's not red, but rather blue.)
- Das ist rot, **aber** nicht mein Lieblingsfarbe. (That's red, but not my favorite color.)

## Forming Questions

**Yes/No questions (verb first):**
- **Sprichst** du Deutsch? (Do you speak German?)
- **Hast** du einen Bruder? (Do you have a brother?)
- **Können** wir gehen? (Can we go?)
- **Ist** er Student? (Is he a student?)

**W-questions (question word + verb in Position 2):**

| Question word | Meaning | Example |
|--------------|---------|---------|
| Was? | What? | Was machst du? (What are you doing?) |
| Wer? | Who? (Nom) | Wer ist das? (Who is that?) |
| Wen? | Whom? (Akk) | Wen siehst du? (Whom do you see?) |
| Wem? | To whom? (Dat) | Wem gibst du das? (To whom do you give that?) |
| Wo? | Where? (location) | Wo wohnst du? (Where do you live?) |
| Wohin? | Where to? (direction) | Wohin gehst du? (Where are you going?) |
| Woher? | Where from? | Woher kommst du? (Where do you come from?) |
| Wann? | When? | Wann kommst du? (When are you coming?) |
| Warum? | Why? | Warum lernst du Deutsch? (Why are you learning German?) |
| Wie? | How? | Wie heißt du? (What's your name?) |
| Wie viel(e)? | How much/many? | Wie viele Geschwister hast du? |
| Welch-? | Which? | Welches Buch liest du? (Which book are you reading?) |

## Relative Clauses (Relativsätze)

Relative clauses add information about a noun. They are introduced by a relative pronoun that matches the gender and number of the noun it refers to, but takes its case from its function WITHIN the relative clause.

**Relative pronouns (same as definite articles, except dative plural and all genitive):**

| Case | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter | Plural |
|------|-----------|----------|--------|--------|
| Nom | der | die | das | die |
| Akk | den | die | das | die |
| Dat | dem | der | dem | denen |
| Gen | dessen | deren | dessen | deren |

**The verb goes to the END of the relative clause (it's a subordinate clause):**

- Der Mann, **der** dort **steht**, ist mein Lehrer. (The man who is standing there is my teacher. — der = Nom. masc.)
- Das Buch, **das** ich **lese**, ist interessant. (The book that I'm reading is interesting. — das = Akk. neuter)
- Die Frau, **der** ich **helfe**, ist meine Nachbarin. (The woman whom I help is my neighbor. — der = Dat. fem. because helfen takes dative)
- Der Film, **den** wir gestern **gesehen haben**, war gut. (The film that we saw yesterday was good. — den = Akk. masc.)
- Die Stadt, **in der** ich **wohne**, ist klein. (The city in which I live is small. — der = Dat. fem. after in)

Form relative clauses:
1. Das ist der Mann. Er wohnt neben mir. → Das ist der Mann, **der** neben mir **wohnt**.

3. Die Frau ist nett. Ich arbeite mit der Frau. → Die Frau, **mit der** ich **arbeite**, ist nett.

# Passive Voice and Konjunktiv II

## Passive Voice (Das Passiv)

The passive voice shifts focus from who does something to what is being done. It is formed with **werden + past participle**.

**Present passive:** Das Buch **wird gelesen**. (The book is being read.)
**Past passive (Präteritum):** Das Buch **wurde gelesen**. (The book was read.)
**Perfekt passive:** Das Buch **ist gelesen worden**. (The book has been read.)
- Note: The past participle of werden in passive is **worden** (not "geworden").

**Examples:**
- Der Kuchen wird von meiner Mutter gebacken. (The cake is baked by my mother.)
- Das Haus wurde 1950 gebaut. (The house was built in 1950.)
- Deutsch wird in vielen Ländern gesprochen. (German is spoken in many countries.)
- Die E-Mail ist schon geschickt worden. (The email has already been sent.)

**"Von" (by) for the agent:** Das Buch wird **von dem Lehrer** erklärt. (The book is explained by the teacher.)

## Konjunktiv II (Subjunctive II)

The Konjunktiv II is used for hypothetical situations, wishes, polite requests, and conditions contrary to fact. It corresponds to "would," "could," and "if...were" in English.

## Common Konjunktiv II Forms

For most verbs, use **würde + infinitive** (would + verb):

| Person | würde |
|--------|-------|
| ich | würde |
| du | würdest |
| er/sie/es | würde |
| wir | würden |
| ihr | würdet |
| sie/Sie | würden |

- Ich **würde** gern nach Japan **fliegen**. (I would like to fly to Japan.)
- Was **würdest** du **machen**? (What would you do?)
- Wir **würden** gern **kommen**. (We would like to come.)

**However, for sein, haben, werden, modal verbs, and a few others, the single-word Konjunktiv II is preferred:**

| Infinitive | Konjunktiv II (ich) | English |
|-----------|--------------------:|---------|
| sein | wäre | would be |
| haben | hätte | would have |
| werden | würde | would become |
| können | könnte | could |
| müssen | müsste | would have to |
| dürfen | dürfte | might/would be allowed |
| sollen | sollte | should |
| wollen | wollte | would want |
| wissen | wüsste | would know |
| geben | gäbe | would give (es gäbe = there would be) |
| kommen | käme | would come |
| gehen | ginge | would go |

## Uses of Konjunktiv II

**1. Hypothetical conditions (Wenn-Sätze):**
- **Wenn** ich reich **wäre**, **würde** ich um die Welt **reisen**. (If I were rich, I would travel around the world.)
- **Wenn** ich Zeit **hätte**, **würde** ich mehr **lesen**. (If I had time, I would read more.)
- **Wenn** ich Deutsch **könnte**, **würde** ich in Deutschland **arbeiten**. (If I could speak German, I would work in Germany.)

**2. Wishes:**
- Ich **wäre** gern in Deutschland. (I would like to be in Germany.)
- Ich **hätte** gern ein neues Auto. (I would like to have a new car.)
- **Wenn** ich doch fliegen **könnte**! (If only I could fly!)

**3. Polite requests (very common):**
- **Könnten** Sie mir bitte helfen? (Could you please help me?)
- **Hätten** Sie einen Moment Zeit? (Would you have a moment?)
- Ich **hätte** gern einen Kaffee. (I would like a coffee.)
- **Würden** Sie bitte das Fenster öffnen? (Would you please open the window?)
- **Dürfte** ich Sie etwas fragen? (Might I ask you something?)

**4. Advice:**
- An deiner Stelle **würde** ich mehr lernen. (In your place, I would study more.)
- Du **solltest** früher ins Bett gehen. (You should go to bed earlier.)

## Als ob / Als wenn (As if)

After "als ob" or "als wenn," use Konjunktiv II:
- Er tut so, **als ob** er nichts **wüsste**. (He acts as if he knew nothing.)
- Sie sieht aus, **als ob** sie krank **wäre**. (She looks as if she were sick.)

## Practice

Write five hypothetical sentences:
1. Wenn ich... wäre, würde ich...
2. Wenn ich... hätte, würde ich...
3. Wenn ich... könnte, würde ich...
And three polite requests using Konjunktiv II.

# Word Formation: Compound Nouns, Prefixes, and Suffixes

## Compound Nouns (Komposita)

One of the most distinctive features of German is its ability to create compound nouns by combining two or more words. There is theoretically no limit to compound length.

**The rule:** The LAST word determines the gender and meaning category; earlier words modify it.

| Compound | Components | Gender | Meaning |
|----------|-----------|--------|---------|
| der Handschuh | Hand (hand) + Schuh (shoe) | der (Schuh) | glove |
| der Staubsauger | Staub (dust) + Sauger (sucker) | der (Sauger) | vacuum cleaner |
| das Krankenhaus | Kranken (sick) + Haus (house) | das (Haus) | hospital |
| der Kühlschrank | kühl (cool) + Schrank (cabinet) | der (Schrank) | refrigerator |
| das Flugzeug | Flug (flight) + Zeug (thing/stuff) | das (Zeug) | airplane |
| der Schlüssel | (from schließen = to close) | der | key |
| das Schlafzimmer | Schlaf (sleep) + Zimmer (room) | das (Zimmer) | bedroom |
| die Geburtstagsfeier | Geburtstag (birthday) + Feier (celebration) | die (Feier) | birthday party |
| der Briefkasten | Brief (letter) + Kasten (box) | der (Kasten) | mailbox |
| das Rathaus | Rat (council) + Haus (house) | das (Haus) | town hall |
| die Sonnenbrillle | Sonne (sun) + Brille (glasses) | die (Brille) | sunglasses |
| der Regenschirm | Regen (rain) + Schirm (screen/shield) | der (Schirm) | umbrella |

**Linking letters:** Sometimes an -s-, -n-, -en-, or -er- is inserted between components for pronunciation: die Geburtstag**s**feier, die Sonnen**n**brille.

**Famous long compound:** Donaudampfschifffahrtsgesellschaftskapitän (Danube steamship company captain) — technically a valid word!

## Verb Prefixes That Change Meaning

German verbs frequently use prefixes to create new meanings:

| Base verb | Prefixed form | Meaning change |
|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| stehen (stand) | verstehen (understand) | |
| | aufstehen (get up) | |
| | bestehen (pass/exist) | |
| | entstehen (originate) | |
| kommen (come) | bekommen (receive) | |
| | ankommen (arrive) | |
| | mitkommen (come along) | |
| | zurückkommen (come back) | |
| schreiben (write) | beschreiben (describe) | |
| | aufschreiben (write down) | |
| | unterschreiben (sign) | |

## Common Suffixes

| Suffix | Gender | English equivalent | Example |
|--------|--------|-------------------|---------|
| -ung | feminine | -tion/-ment | die Bildung (education), die Wohnung (apartment) |
| -heit | feminine | -ness/-ity | die Freiheit (freedom), die Gesundheit (health) |
| -keit | feminine | -ness/-ity | die Möglichkeit (possibility), die Freundlichkeit (friendliness) |
| -schaft | feminine | -ship | die Freundschaft (friendship), die Mannschaft (team) |
| -lich | — | -ly/-ful | freundlich (friendly), möglich (possible), glücklich (happy) |
| -ig | — | -y | sonnig (sunny), traurig (sad), lustig (funny) |
| -bar | — | -able | essbar (edible), lesbar (readable), machbar (feasible) |
| -er | masculine | -er (person) | der Lehrer (teacher), der Fahrer (driver) |
| -in | feminine | -er (female) | die Lehrerin (female teacher), die Fahrerin (female driver) |
| -chen/-lein | neuter | diminutive | das Häuschen (little house), das Büchlein (little book) |

## Practice

Break these compound nouns into components and explain their meaning:
1. Haustür (Haus + Tür = house door / front door)
2. Schwimmbad (Schwimm + Bad = swimming bath / pool)
3. Geburtsort (Geburt + Ort = birth place / birthplace)
Then create three new compounds by combining nouns you know.

English speakers who approach German systematically can leverage these similarities while focusing their efforts on the areas of genuine difference.
